title: Crops and the Farming Year
hint: Wheat, barley, corn, canola, hay and straw; plough, sow, harvest; describing a process with the passive
why: bread, cereal, cooking oil and chips all start in a farmer's field. Knowing the main crops and the steps of the farming year helps you read food labels and news stories, and the language for describing a process (first, then, the seeds are sown) is useful in any job.
understand: passive for a process: The seeds are sown in April.
able: name the crops that grow in your country and say what they are used for
describe the farming year, season by season
explain a simple process step by step

The seeds are sown in April. (sow, sowed, sown)
The wheat is harvest in August.
At first, the field is ploughed. Then the seeds are sown.
First, the field is ploughed. Then the seeds are sown.
The cows sleep on straw. (hay is food; straw is bedding)

We eat corn on the cob. / We eat an ear of corn.

exercises.title: Reading
exercises.text:
A year on a Prairie grain farm

My family has farmed near Swift Current, Saskatchewan, for four generations. We grow wheat, canola and lentils on about two thousand acres.

Our year really begins in April, when the snow melts. First, the machines are checked and repaired. Then, in early May, the seeds are sown. We don't plough any more: the seeds go straight into the stubble (the short stems left from last year's crop). This keeps water in the soil, and on the Prairies water is precious.

In June and July we watch the sky. With too little rain, the crop is small. Hail can destroy a whole field in ten minutes. The fields are sprayed once or twice to control the weeds.

Harvest starts in late August. The wheat is cut with a combine, and the grain is taken by truck to our storage bins. Finally, in late September, the canola is harvested. After that, the grain is sold, and we can relax a little.

In winter we plan next year's crops. We rotate them, so a field of wheat this year will be canola or lentils next year.
exercises.intro: Read the farmer's story. Then type the missing word from the text, and press Check.

items.why: Paragraph 2: sowing into the stubble 'keeps water in the soil'.

exercises.title: Speaking
items: What are the main crops in your country? What are they used for?

parts.rule:
Watch out

  • First (or Firstly) is for the first step. At first means “at the beginning, but not later”: At first I hated farm work, but now I love it.
  • Finally is for the last step. In the end means “after a long time or many problems”.
parts.intro: Where does each phrase go in a description of a process? Sort them.

chips.why: First introduces the first step: First, the field is ploughed.
To begin with = first: To begin with, the machines are checked.
Firstly is a slightly more formal way to say first.
Then introduces the next step: Then the seeds are sown.
Next introduces the next step: Next, the crop is sprayed.
After that introduces a later step: After that, the grain is dried.
Once that's done = when the last step is finished, the next one starts.
Finally introduces the last step: Finally, the grain is stored.
Lastly = finally: the last step in a list or process.
In the end = at last, often after a long time or problems: In the end, the rain stopped.

items.q: The seeds are sow in April.
items.why: Passive needs the past participle: sow, sowed, sown. The seeds are sown in April.

items.q: The wheat is harvest in August.
items.why: Passive: is + past participle. The wheat is harvested in August.

items.q: Finally, the grain is stored in the silo.
items.why: Correct: Finally for the last step, and the passive is stored.

items.q: Farmers grows potatoes in this valley.
items.why: Farmers is plural, so the verb has no -s: Farmers grow potatoes.

items.q: At first, the field is ploughed, and then the seeds are sown.
items.why: For the first step of a process, say First. At first means 'at the beginning, but not later'.

teacher.purpose: give general learners the words for the main crops and the farming year (plough, sow, spray, harvest, store, rotate), the difference between hay and straw, and the language for describing a process: sequencing words and the present simple passive (The seeds are sown in April).
teacher.before: find a photo of a field of wheat, a field of yellow canola, and bales of hay or straw. Optional: a short video of a combine harvester at work (search “combine harvester wheat harvest”); students who grew up in cities have often never seen one.
plan: The three warm-up questions. The breakfast question works well: toast = wheat, cereal = corn or oats, oil = canola or sunflower.
Crops first, with your photos. Then the verbs: act them out in order (plough, sow, spray, harvest, store). Then the process box: show how the passive keeps the crop at the front of the sentence.
Matching, then the process sentences. In Exercise 2, ask for the past participle every time: sown, ploughed, harvested, stored.
Do one together and set the other for home.
The Prairie grain farm. Before the questions, ask the student to put the year in order: spring, summer, harvest, winter. Then underline every passive verb (there are eight).
Question 2 is the core: from field to plate, step by step. Insist on a sequencing word for every step, and at least two passives.
Exercise 7 Part A together; Part B at home.
pron: plough /plaʊ/: rhymes with cow. The -ough spelling confuses everyone (though, through, rough). North American spelling plow shows the sound better.
sow /səʊ/, sown /səʊn/: rhyme with go and grown. A female pig, sow /saʊ/, rhymes with cow (Lesson 1).
harvest /ˈhɑːvɪst/: stress on HAR. harvested has an extra syllable: /ˈhɑːvɪstɪd/.
Past participles with -ed: ploughed /plaʊd/ and stored /stɔːd/ are one syllable; harvested, rotated, planted add a syllable after t.
mistakes: hay vs straw: hay is food (dried grass, green and smells sweet); straw is bedding (dry yellow stems, empty inside). Many languages use one word for both.
corn: in the UK corn can mean any grain (a cornfield may be wheat). In North America corn is always maize. Spanish maíz, French maïs: say corn in Canada and the US.
sow / sew / so: all /səʊ/. Sow seeds, sew clothes. Students often write sewn for sown.
At first vs First: At first means “in the beginning (but it changed later)”. For steps, use First or Firstly. In the end vs Finally: in the end suggests a long wait or problems.
The passive: learners drop the be (The wheat harvested in August) or use the base form (is harvest). Make them say the full form aloud: is harvested.
grain is uncountable for the crop (a lot of grain); a grain of rice is one seed. crop is countable: two crops a year.
harvest is a verb and a noun: We harvest in August. The harvest was good this year. In the UK harvest also means autumn festivals (harvest festival).
uk_us: In the UK, corn can mean any grain crop.
Canola is a Canadian name (from Canada + oil). Canada is the biggest grower.
Useful if the student talks about potatoes.
adapt: Six crops (wheat, corn, potatoes, oats, hay, straw) and five verbs (plough, sow, grow, harvest, store). Passive with is/are + past participle for three or four steps.
All crops; add yield, stubble, combine harvester, irrigate, fertilise, a bumper crop, cash crop. Passive with modal verbs: The grain must be dried before it can be stored.
Describe one food from field to plate in four steps.
Compare farming in two climates, or explain why crop rotation or no-till farming helps the soil.
prompts: Main crops in your country. Follow up: “Where are they grown?” “Are they exported?” Good chances for the passive: Rice is grown in the south.
From field to plate. Follow up after each step: “And then what happens?” “Who does that?” Correct missing be in the passive gently by repeating the sentence correctly.
Seasons in the countryside. Follow up: “What colours are the fields then?” “Is there a harvest festival or holiday?”
Growing your own food. Follow up: “When would you plant it?” “What could go wrong?” This leads into Lesson 7 (weather and problems).

bank.q: Most of the bread in Canada is made from ___ grown on the Prairies.
bank.why: Bread is made from flour, and flour comes from wheat.

bank.q: In summer the fields turn bright yellow when the ___ is in flower.
bank.why: Canola (UK rapeseed) has bright yellow flowers. Its seeds give cooking oil.

bank.q: The horses eat ___ in winter, when there is no fresh grass.
bank.why: Hay is dried grass, so animals eat it. Straw is for bedding.

bank.q: The carrots ___ in March and picked in July.
bank.why: Passive for a process: are + past participle. The carrots are sown in March.

bank.q: The corn ___ in October, when the cobs are hard and dry.
bank.why: The corn doesn't do the harvesting: it is harvested. Use is + past participle.

bank.q: ___, the apples are washed. Then they are packed into boxes.
bank.why: First introduces the first step of a process. At first means 'in the beginning, but not later'.

bank.q: Wheat is ___ in many countries, from China to Argentina.
bank.why: Passive: is + past participle. Grow, grew, grown: Wheat is grown in many countries.

bank.q: The potatoes are dug up, washed and ___ stored in a cool, dark shed.
bank.why: Finally introduces the last step, after dug up and washed.

bank.q: After the wheat harvest, the farmer makes bales of ___ for the animals to sleep on.
bank.why: Straw is the dry stems left after the harvest. Animals sleep on it.

bank.q: A tall round building for storing grain is called a ___.
bank.why: A silo is a tall round tower where grain is stored.

bank.q: Sow, sowed, ___: The seeds have been sown.
bank.why: Sow has two past participles, sown and sowed. Sown is more common.

bank.q: In the US and Canada, maize is called ___.
bank.why: Maize is the British word. In North America it is called corn.

bank.q: Growing a different crop in a field each year is called crop ___.
bank.why: Crop rotation keeps the soil healthy. The verb is rotate.

bank.q: The rice is plant by hand in the wet fields.
bank.why: Passive: is + past participle. The rice is planted by hand.

bank.q: The cows sleep on clean hay every night.
bank.why: Animals sleep on straw. Hay is food.

bank.q: When the barley is dry, it is cut with a combine harvester.
bank.why: Correct: When + step, and the passive is cut.

bank.q: Then the grain is taken to the mill and made into flour.
bank.why: Correct: Then for the next step, and two passives: is taken, made.

bank.a: The oats are harvested at the end of summer.
alt: At the end of summer the oats are harvested.
bank.why: Passive: The oats + are harvested + when.

bank.a: After that, the grain is dried and stored.
bank.why: Sequencing word first, then the passive: After that, the grain is dried and stored.

bank.a: Which crops are grown near your home town?
bank.why: Passive question: Which crops + are grown + where?
